old_title: Ukraine-Russia live: Putin says peace 'on the table' - yet warns of further strikes
new_title: Ukraine latest: Germany urges Russia to stop 'dangerous escalation' against Nato

Russian president Vladimir Putin has said all proposals for a settlement to the war in Ukraine remain "on the table," but has warned Kyiv to prepare for a sustained wave of retaliatory strikes.
Addressing journalists in St. Petersburg on Friday, the Russian leader claimed Moscow was ready to resume peace negotiations after his party secured a record supermajority Russia's parliamentary elections this week.
However, Putin accused Ukrainian forces of intentionally derailing potential diplomatic channels with long-range drone strikes on polling stations during the voting period.
Dismissing Kyiv's recent military operations, Putin said: "They are the ones who started it... Everywhere, on every front. Are these playthings, child's play?
"[Ukraine] should therefore be made to feel Russia's retaliatory strikes and understand that no provocative actions ... will work. They're only making things worse for themselves."
While insisting that ceasefire frameworks and diplomatic solutions remain possible, Putin stressed that Moscow will first carefully assess what best serves its own national interests before agreeing to any terms.
The comments come as Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed in Washington that he asked US president Donald Trump to press Chinese President Xi Jinping to use Beijing's leverage over Moscow.
Four dead in Russian strikes across Ukraine
Russian attacks killed four people across Ukraine on Saturday, officials said, as the aerial war between Moscow and Kyiv intensified.
Russia has hammered Ukraine with cruise and ballistic missiles, powerful glide bombs and jet-powered drones in recent weeks while front line progress has slowed.
Two women in Zaporizhzhia died when they were trapped beneath the rubble of their destroyed home, Zaporizhzhia's regional military administration said. A separate Russian attack on the city of Sumy also killed two people, local officials said.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, two people were injured in the Kyiv region overnight after a Russian drone attack caused a fire at a warehouse in the Boryspil district. Russian drones also hit several districts in the Ukrainian capital itself, injuring four and damaging residential and office buildings, officials said.
Russia's defence ministry said on Saturday that its attack on Kyiv had damaged a data centre that supported both cellphone internet services and Starlink satellite communication systems.
Putin discusses energy cooperation with Serbian president
Russian president Vladimir Putin discussed the Ukraine war and energy cooperation with Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic during a phone call, the Kremlin said on Saturday.
Vucic has described Serbia as "neutral" when it comes to the Ukraine conflict. The country has long held close relations with Russia but has also supported UN resolutions condemning Putin's aggression.
Three killed in Ukrainian attack on Krasnodar region, says Russia
Three people were killed and two injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Krasnodar region, local authorities there have said.
A local task force said fires at industrial sites that had broken out as a result of the attack had been extinguished.
Zelensky says he got Trump's OK for Patriot licences
The Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky says Donald Trump confirmed this week that he had made a final decision to allow Kyiv to get licences to produce Patriot air defence systems.
Ukraine is desperate for more of the American-made air defence systems that are needed to stop Russia's ballistic missiles, but they have been in short supply since the war in Iran started on 28 February.
Trump had said in July that he would allow Ukraine to make its own Patriots but later appeared to be reconsidering the move.
Zelensky urges Trump to get China to help end Russia's invasion
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky says he asked Donald Trump to press China's Xi Jinping to use Beijing's influence over Moscow and end the war on his country.
Zelensky told reporters late on Friday that he has not yet received feedback from the White House about Trump's talks with Xi, but expects to learn the outcome.
Nato countries have called China a "decisive enabler" of Russian president Vladimir Putin's invasion.
Zelensky was also in the US this week on a trip coinciding with the UN General Assembly. He met with Trump on Tuesday.
Zelensky met with US senators and Congress members during his trip and said he thanked them for their bipartisan support in passing a powerful sanctions bill aimed at Moscow last month. Trump signed the bill into law last week but hasn't enacted the measures yet.
Inside the real war games as Europe readies for an attack by Russia
As warnings increase about a Russian attack on a Nato country, real-world war-games, are happening all the time. But the real danger is the potential for hysteria, fear and miscalculation to turn a shadow war into something much worse, writes Owen Matthews:
Little movement on Ukraine peace after turbulent week of UN diplomacy
The UN General Assembly concluded on Friday after a week of speeches, meetings and hallway diplomacy.
While they reached no breakthroughs onthe world's most intractable conflicts, talks on the Iran and Ukraine wars inched forward.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio held talks with Russia's foreign minister Sergei Lavrov, after which he said Ukraine and Russia had both voiced an interest in a limited ceasefire involving grain and energy-related targets.
Ukraine and its allies are racing to secure these limited agreements before winter, fearing renewed Russian strikes on power and heating facilities.
But hours after Rubio spoke on Wednesday, Lavrov addressed the Security Council meeting on Ukraine, showing no indication Russia was prepared to engage on any subject. "Europe, whatever it thinks, just wants to get a pause, and it wants to use it to pump the Kyiv regime with weapons," Lavrov said.
UN refugee chief urges Security Council to do more to end wars
The UN's refugee chief used his first speech at the Security Council yesterday to call for a renewed focus on ending conflicts and crises, so that more than 117 million people forced to flee their homes can return and don't spend generations displaced in a foreign country.
The Ukraine war was just one of the conflicts cited by Barham Salih, who told the Council's 15 members that they have "a unique responsibility to help make peace possible."
He said the conflict started by Vladimir Putin's invasion in 2022 had displaced millions inside the country and sent millions more fleeing to other countries.
"For the millions of people forced from their homes - and the millions more who should never have to flee - I urge you to use that responsibility," the former refugee, who was president of Iraq from 2018 to 2022, told the meeting on the sidelines of the annual UN gathering of world leaders.
Drone hits Russia's Ilsky oil refinery
Ukrainian drones reportedly targeted the Ilsky oil refinery in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, causing a fire at the facility.
Local governor Veniamin Kondratiev said that the Ukrainian drones targeted Seversky district, which houses one of the largest oil-processing facilities in southern Russia.
The extent of the damage to the refinery and casualties were not immediately known.
Government warned Homes for Ukraine funding cut may 'send wrong message to Putin'
Planned government cuts to the Homes for Ukraine Scheme could "send the wrong message to Putin" by giving the impression that Western support for Kyiv is faltering, a Conservative former defence secretary has warned.
Starting from 1 January, monthly "thank-you" payments for households hosting Ukrainian refugees are set to drop from £350 to £100.
Local authority funding to support the initiative will also be scaled back on the same date, falling from £5,900 per guest to £3,300 per arrival.

Germany has urged Vladimir Putin to stop Russia's "dangerous path of escalation" against it and other Nato countries and find a peaceful end to the war in Ukraine.
The German foreign minister Johann Wadephul met with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Saturday, although Lavrov later said the talks led to no meaningful breakthrough.
Lavrov dismissed Wadephul's concerns and instead accused Germany of prolonging the war by supporting Ukraine. In his speech later to the General Assembly, he said: "Does Berlin understand what this could lead to? Didn't they not learn the lessons of World War II?"
Meanwhile, both Russia and Ukraine ramped up their aerial attacks on Saturday, with at least 10 people killed across both countries, despite Donald Trump's plea for a peace deal.
Mr Trump told Zelensky to make a deal with Vladimir Putin to end the war at the UN General Assembly earlier this week in New York.
"You know what I want him to do? Make a deal," the president told Fox News. "I want him to settle with Putin and I want Putin to settle with him."
Two dead in Russian strikes on Kyiv and Odesa
Russian strikes on Ukraine killed at least two people overnight into Sunday, officials said.
In Kyiv, a man was found dead after a Russian drone hit a non-residential building overnight, according to Ukraine's emergency service.
Another drone struck a single-story vehicle repair shop, leaving firefighters battling the blaze into early Sunday.
Russian forces also struck Ukraine's southern Odesa region, which surrounds the country's main Black Sea port, multiple times overnight into Sunday, killing one person and injuring two others, according to the head of the local military administration, Oleh Kiper.
Inside the real war games as Europe readies for an attack by Russia
Sky's docu-drama The Wargame has landed right in the middle of a time of real-world crisis. But the true danger is the potential for hysteria, fear and miscalculation to turn a shadow war into something much worse, as Owen Matthews explains:
Europe's far-right turmoil is only the beginning - all the signs point to worse to come
John Kampfner writes about the terrifying surge of the far right across Europe, and why it's only good news for Russia:
Russia says it struck military infrastructure and vessel in Ukraine
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday its forces had carried out overnight drone strikes on logistics centres, port and transport infrastructure, as well as communications centres and vessels that Moscow said were linked to the Ukrainian military.
The ministry said the strikes hit a data centre in Kyiv, logistic hubs in the Kyiv and Odesa regions, two drone storages in Mykolaiv, headquarters of a naval base as well as of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine and four military storages in the Kiliya port, and a cargo ship carrying military and dual-use goods to the port of Odesa.
Russia uses UN address to criticise West and deny isolation
Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov used his speech yesterday at the UN General Assembly and a subsequent news conference to blame the West for undermining European security, despite Russia being the aggressor in its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Lavrov claimed the West "aspires to inflict strategic defeat on Russia - but these aspirations will result in the war mongers being led into a strategic dead end."
He also claimed the US specifically had "destroyed the European security system and created a Russophobic regime in Kyiv".
Moscow has repeatedly sought to stress that it maintains a strong position on the global stage despite its war on Ukraine and isolation from the West.
Writing on her personal Telegram channel, Maria Zakharova, chief spokesperson for Russia's foreign ministry, claimed that "tens of diplomats" had come to meet Lavrov to "shake his hand and thank Russia" at the UN.
An overwhelming majority of General Assembly member nations have repeatedly condemned Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Voters in Switzerland decide on right-wing party's proposal to tighten neutrality rules
Voters are taking part in a referendum in Switzerland today on a proposal to strengthen the country's neutrality rules.
The referendum is supported by a right-wing populist party that insists the Swiss government has gravitated too close to the European Union and Nato, notably over Russia's war in Ukraine.
Backers of the plan, championed by the Swiss People's Party, want Switzerland to reinforce its commitment to neutrality that has been enshrined in the constitution since the mid-19th century and has faced years of debate over what that neutrality really means.
The party, which has the most seats in parliament and counts some members with pro-Russia leanings, has bristled over the Swiss federal government's decision to denounce Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and join EU sanctions against Moscow.
The measure would prohibit the government from joining sanctions against any belligerent country except sanctions approved by the United Nations. Russia has been shielded from such measures because it wields a veto on the UN Security Council as one of its five permanent members.
Switzerland is not a member of any military alliance. Passage would also bar the Swiss government from cooperating with any alliance - as it has with Nato for three decades, including through joint exercises - except in cases where it faces a direct threat.
Germany says relations cannot improve with Russia unless Putin moves to end war
The meeting between German and Russian foreign ministers on Saturday, at Germany's Johann Wadephul's request, came just before Sergey Lavrov addressed world leaders, where he also criticised the militarisation of Japan.
He made clear that Russia will veto any attempt by Germany and Japan for permanent seats on the Security Council, the UN's most powerful body. The two nations fought Russia, Britain and the United States in World War II.
A German delegation official said that during their meeting, Wadephul called on Russia to abandon its "dangerous path of escalation" toward Germany, Europe and the Nato alliance. Ties between Russia and Germany have soured in recent weeks, following an attempted drone attack last month at Leipzig airport - Germany has blamed the incident on Russia - and tit-for-tat responses that followed.
Wadephul expressed openness to a better relationship but said it required a genuine willingness from Russia's leadership to end the war in Ukraine, according to the official.
Russia's top diplomat rejects German calls to stop 'dangerous escalation'
Russia's top diplomat rejected German calls to ease off its "dangerous path of escalation" toward the country, instead accusing Germany of being Ukraine's main sponsor and seeking to be a leading military power in Europe.
"Does Berlin understand what this could lead to?' Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov asked in his speech at the UN General Assembly's annual gathering of world leaders. "Didn't they not learn the lessons of World War II?"
Lavrov was dismissive after the German and Russian foreign ministers met Saturday on the sidelines of the meeting, holding what's believed to be the first such tête-à-tête since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"He simply reiterated his official public position condemning Russia," Lavrov said. "You can judge for yourself whether that counts as dialogue or not."
